source.title_on_document: Effects of Personalized Generative AI on Student Creativity: Evidence from Creative Performance, Self-efficacy, and Attention Allocation

supplement.where: The chapter refers to no supplementary material, online appendix, or data repository.

paper_design_summary: Sixty-two university students in a lab each did two Product Improvement Tasks (three improvement ideas for a common product), one with standard ChatGPT-4 and one with a personalized GPT-4 tutor (Mr. Ranedeer), with the order counterbalanced (31 per order). Two trained raters blind to condition scored each solution on quality, elaboration, and originality (1-5); the paper also measured self-reported creative self-efficacy and eye-tracking metrics, and compared conditions with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

studies.label: Within-subject lab experiment: personalized GAI tutor (Mr. Ranedeer) vs standard ChatGPT-4 on the Product Improvement Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two AI conditions (standard ChatGPT-4 first vs personalized Mr. Ranedeer first); every participant used both. The paper says the order was counterbalanced but does not say participants were randomly allocated to an order. It also does not say which product was paired with which condition.
assignment.quote: A counterbalanced design was used: half completed the first task with ChatGPT-4 and the second with Mr. Ranedeer, while the other half followed the reverse order.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 Procedure and Fig. 2

arms.name: Personalized GAI (Mr. Ranedeer)
arms.description: GPT-4-powered tutor customized on OpenAI's 'Explore GPTs' platform; three stages: students set learning preferences and co-design a plan, Socratic heuristic questioning, then solution elaboration with goal-aligned feedback and strategic prompts.

arms.name: Standard GAI (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 giving generic feedback in two stages: broad suggestions in response to queries, then solution generation on request; minimal structure.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper states 62 participants and reports no exclusions or dropouts; it does not print a separate analysis N. Fig. 2 shows 31 per order group (15 undergraduates/16 graduates; 17 undergraduates/14 graduates). Each participant appears in both arms, so the arm counts are the same 62 people.
participants.who: 32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students, 33.9% male, aged 18-27 (M = 22.6, SD = 2.5), from social sciences, life sciences, and technical disciplines; almost all had prior GAI experience; compensated.
participants.country: not_stated (all author affiliations are in China; the paper does not name the participants' country or university)
participants.quote: Sixty-two students (32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students; 33.9% male) participated in the study.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Fig. 2

ai_tool.name_model: Both arms built on OpenAI GPT-4: standard ChatGPT-4 vs Mr. Ranedeer, a custom GPT tutor made via OpenAI's 'Explore GPTs' platform
ai_tool.how_used: Participants worked in a split-screen layout with the AI chat (OpenAI web interface) on one side and a workspace where they typed their solutions on the other. In the standard arm ChatGPT-4 gave broad suggestions and generated solutions on request. In the personalized arm the tutor first set preferences and a plan, then asked Socratic questions, then gave goal-aligned feedback and refinement/elaboration cues. Both arms could receive AI-generated content.

task.description: Product Improvement Task (Torrance, 1966): propose three solutions, as original and useful as possible, to improve a common product (e.g., a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee machine), one product per task, using the assigned GAI tool. It is a product-idea task taken from the Torrance tests.
task.duration: About 17 min (SD = 7) in the standard condition and 20 min (SD = 6) in the personalized condition; five-minute break between tasks

outcomes.name: Creative performance: quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained raters blind to condition rated each solution on a 1-5 scale; quality = extent to which a solution addresses the task objective; solutions presented in randomized order; Cronbach's alpha = 0.88; final score = average of the two raters. The paper does not describe the raters' expertise.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 3.50, SD = 1.00 vs standard M = 3.08, SD = 1.12; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = .001; r = .42 (N = 62 within-subject; no Z printed for this outcome)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 384), Fig. 4A

outcomes.name: Creative performance: elaboration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two blind trained raters, 1-5 scale; elaboration = amount of detail provided; Cronbach's alpha = 0.90; average of two raters.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 3.58, SD = 1.17 vs standard M = 2.48, SD = 1.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank p < .001; r = .62
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 384), Fig. 4A

outcomes.name: Creative performance: originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two blind trained raters, 1-5 scale; originality = novelty of the idea; Cronbach's alpha = 0.86; average of two raters.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 2.92, SD = 1.15 vs standard M = 3.13, SD = 1.27; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = .098; r = .18 (point estimate lower under personalized)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 384), Fig. 4A

company_involvement.description: No company authors or funding stated; the tools are OpenAI's ChatGPT-4 and a custom GPT built on OpenAI's platform.

eligibility.reason: Within-person comparison of two GAI configurations (personalized tutor vs standard ChatGPT-4), an ai_design contrast with no no-AI arm. Order was counterbalanced (31 per order, Fig. 2), but the paper never says participants were randomly allocated to an order, which the codebook requires for a within-person design; criterion 1 is therefore unclear. 62 students participated and no exclusions are reported (above 50). Outcomes are blind-rater scores of the written solutions (quality, elaboration, originality).

one_line_finding: With 62 students in a within-subject lab study, a personalized GPT-4 tutor raised rated quality (3.50 vs 3.08, p = .001, r = .42) and elaboration (3.58 vs 2.48, p < .001, r = .62) relative to standard ChatGPT-4, with no clear difference in originality (2.92 vs 3.13, p = .098) (PDF p. 8, Sect. 4.1).
open_questions: Was the order of conditions randomly allocated, or assigned by another rule? The paper says only 'counterbalanced'.
Which product (stuffed bunny vs portable coffee machine) went with which condition, and was product counterbalanced against condition? Not stated, so product may be confounded with condition.
Are the creativity scores participant-level means over three solutions? The paired Wilcoxon tests imply participant-level data, but the paper does not say how the three solutions were aggregated.
Fig. 4 caption says error bars are SDs; in panel B the self-efficacy bars look far narrower than the printed SDs (0.99 and 1.19), so the figure may show SEs.
notes: Creative self-efficacy (7-point self-report, measured before each task) and eye-tracking metrics (mean fixation duration, number of transitions; Table 1, PDF p. 9) are not scored on the output and are not listed as outcomes. Self-efficacy: personalized M = 5.24, SD = 0.99 vs standard M = 4.89, SD = 1.19; p = .033; r = .26 (PDF p. 8). Table 2 (PDF p. 10) gives within-condition correlations only. Rater type coded human_raters because the paper calls them 'two trained raters' without stating expertise. Task coded divergent_test because the paper names the Torrance Product Improvement Task; it could also be read as idea_generation (product ideas). AI role coded open_chat because both arms used the OpenAI chat interface; the treatment arm adds a coach-like Socratic stage and refinement feedback. Time on task differed by arm (about 17 vs 20 min).
